title: Rules for the Worst of Times
subject: English

intro: Lesson 61: Non-fiction: the just war tradition and Islam's rules of war. Read the whole text, then answer the questions. Annotate methods and their effects in the margin.

passage.title: Rules for the Worst of Times
paras: War is the opposite of order, yet for centuries people have tried to set rules for it. The just war tradition, developed by thinkers over many centuries, asks three questions.
Before war: is it right to go to war at all? There must be a just cause, such as defending people from attack, and war must be a last resort, used only when every peaceful way has failed.
During war: how must it be fought? Non-combatants, people who are not fighting, must be protected. Force must be proportionate: no more than is needed to achieve a just aim.
After war: how should peace be made? The defeated must be treated fairly, and what was destroyed should be rebuilt.

Islam set limits on war from its beginning. The Qur'an commands: 'Fight... those who fight you, but do not transgress' (al-Baqarah 2:190). The Prophet ﷺ forbade killing women and children, as reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. These limits are part of the faith, not an afterthought: a Muslim soldier answers to Allah even when no court is watching.
Rules do not end cruelty. The poems we study show blunders, cold and grief that no rule prevented. But rules give us a standard, and a standard lets us say clearly when something is wrong.

questions.q: What does 'proportionality' mean in the article?
questions.a: Using no more force than is needed to achieve a just aim.

questions.q: Give one rule of conduct from Islam and its source.
questions.a: Do not transgress (al-Baqarah 2:190), or the Prophet ﷺ forbade killing women and children (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

questions.q: Retrieve: what does 'proportionality' mean in the article?
questions.a: Using no more force than is needed to achieve a just aim.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a PEEDL paragraph: 'Can rules limit the cruelty of war?' Use the article and one poem. Starter: 'Rules can limit war's cruelty because..., however...'
questions.a: A PEEDL paragraph with a judgement, evidence from the article and a poem, and a counter-point.

questions.q: Extend: which part of the tradition does each poem most connect with?
questions.a: Tennyson: during war (orders); Owen: during war (conditions); Weir: after war (families); Satyamurti: during and after (witness).

questions.q: Stretch: why might a faith-based limit be stronger than a law?
questions.a: Because believers answer to Allah even when no court is watching.

questions.q: Which principle protects people who are not fighting?
questions.a: A) protecting non-combatants. Non-combatant protection is about conduct during war.

questions.q: Answer the ponder: can there be rules in war?
questions.a: For example: yes; faith and law set limits to protect the innocent.
